rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3 report the authors' own installation and first-year (June-September 2000) operation of an automated sensor-based irrigation control system in the Padova Botanical Garden. Q2: Section 3.1 and Fig. 6 report that the automated TDT-threshold system terminated irrigation when rainfall raised moisture above the 32% full point, reset go-ahead 6 days after rain, maintained matric potential never below -75 kPa, and that the maximum inefficiency from sensor scanning delay was 0.6 mm. Q3: Section 2.6 and Figs. 6-7: soil water status under the automated regime was assessed both with TDT moisture probes and with independent tensiometers (matric potential), plus TDR on sentinel plants. Q4: Sections 2.5-2.6, Fig. 6: the intermediate variable (root-zone soil moisture and matric potential, water-table depth) through which the automation triggers/terminates irrigation was measured continuously. Q7: Conclusions and Section 3.1: from their own data the authors state the 'average' criterion penalised plants with higher needs and that a criterion accounting for within-sector variability (OR logical) is needed to guarantee water status; Section 2.4 states macro-sectors must be sufficiently homogeneous in water requirement, cover and ET demand for automated management. Q8: Sections 2.4, 3 and 3.1: only 15 probes allowed, single sensor in MS5 and MS6, TDT 5 worked only from end of July, first experimental year only, Landolt index limitations, average criterion did not evaluate plant variability.
rows.notes: The study concerns automated sensor-based scheduling of a sprinkler system; it shows the automation functioned (stopping irrigation after rain, keeping favourable water status) but does not quantify water saved relative to a non-automated baseline, so support for 'conserve water resources' is indirect. Q5: single site (one 2-ha garden, one soil), vegetation types differ within site but not distinct soils/regions. Q6: one 2-ha garden site, treated as single site. Q9: Table 1 gives S.D. for retention curves only; ranges of moisture/potential in Fig. 6 are time-series ranges, not dispersion of the automation result.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3 report the authors' own installation and first-year operation data of an automated irrigation system.
rows.notes: The study's irrigation network consists of about 550 sprinklers controlled by 27 solenoid valves (Section 2.2); no drip irrigation is tested or reported. It shows automated sensor-based control of a sprinkler system in a botanical garden, not any effect of drip irrigation on water conservation.

notes: Full text appears complete (figures described in captions only). Study is a single-site case study of soil-moisture-sensor automation of sprinkler irrigation in a 2-ha botanical garden, first year only.
